own.story: Abel Collin, born in Nottingham in 1653, left money in his will of 1704 for almshouses. Those on Friar Lane, built in 1709, were demolished in 1956 to make way for Maid Marian Way; his charity, the oldest in Nottingham, still has houses in Beeston.

Albert Iremonger.text: Albert Iremonger was a football goalkeeper, county-class cricketer and brother of sportsmen Harry Iremonger and James Iremonger.
Albert Iremonger.title: Albert Iremonger

own.story: Born in Wilford, the 6 ft 5 in goalkeeper played 564 matches for Notts County.[^s1][^s2] In the 1940s he ran the Ferry Inn.[^s1][^s2]

Albert Nelson Bromley.text: Albert Nelson Bromley was an English architect based in Nottingham.
Albert Nelson Bromley.title: Albert Nelson Bromley

own.story: The architect Albert Nelson Bromley designed these houses on Newcastle Drive in 1878, and died here in 1934. His buildings in the city include Boots' stores on Pelham Street and Turney Street.

Arthur Shrewsbury.text: Arthur Shrewsbury was an English cricketer and rugby football administrator. He was widely rated as competing with W. G.
Arthur Shrewsbury.title: Arthur Shrewsbury

own.story: Arthur Shrewsbury, born in New Lenton in 1856, scored his first century at Trent Bridge in 1876 and captained England seven times, the last professional to do so until Len Hutton. Asked whom he would most like in his side, W. G. Grace said: "Give me Arthur."

Augustus Pugin.text: Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin was an English architect, designer, artist and critic with French and Swiss origins. He is principally remembered for his pioneering role in the Gothic Revival style of architecture. Among his best-known work is the interior of the Palace of Westminster and its clock tower nicknamed 'Big Ben'.
Augustus Pugin.title: Augustus Pugin

own.story: Augustus Pugin, who also designed the interior of the Houses of Parliament, designed the cathedral.[^s1][^s2]

Bill Voce.text: Bill Voce was an English cricketer who played for Nottinghamshire and England. As a fast bowler, he was an instrumental part of England's infamous Bodyline strategy in their tour of Australia in 1932–1933 under Douglas Jardine. He was born at Annesley Woodhouse, near Kirkby-in-Ashfield, Nottinghamshire.
Bill Voce.title: Bill Voce

own.story: Bill Voce, born at Annesley Woodhouse in 1909, walked from Hucknall to Trent Bridge hoping for a trial. With Harold Larwood he bowled Bodyline for England, and he later became the county's coach.

Brian Clough.text: Brian Howard Clough was an English football player and manager, primarily known for his successes as a manager with Derby County and Nottingham Forest. He won the European Cup twice with Nottingham Forest and is one of four managers to have won the English league with two different clubs. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest managers of all time.
Brian Clough.title: Brian Clough

own.story: Brian Clough managed Nottingham Forest at the City Ground.[^s1][^s2]

Charles J. Phipps.text: Charles John Phipps was an English architect known for more than forty theatres he designed in the latter half of the nineteenth century. He began his own practice in his native Bath in 1857, designing buildings and furniture in the Gothic Revival style. In 1862 he gained his first theatre commission, the Theatre Royal, Bath, which generally retaining the Georgian character of the original theatre on the site.
Charles J. Phipps.title: C. J. Phipps

own.story: The theatre architect Charles J. Phipps designed the Theatre Royal.[^s1][^s2]

D. H. Lawrence.text: David Herbert Lawrence was an English novelist, short story writer, poet, playwright, literary critic, travel writer, essayist, and painter. His modernist works reflect on modernity, social alienation and industrialisation, while championing sexuality, vitality and instinct.
D. H. Lawrence.title: D. H. Lawrence

own.story: Built between 1877 and 1881 for University College Nottingham, where D. H. Lawrence studied during his teacher-training years.[^s1]

Dorothea Waddingham.text: Dorothea Nancy Waddingham was an English nursing home matron who was convicted of murder.
Dorothea Waddingham.title: Dorothea Waddingham

own.story: Dorothea Waddingham ran a nursing home in her house here, 32 Devon Drive. She was hanged in 1936 for poisoning two of her patients, Louisa Baguley and her daughter Ada, with morphine.

Feargus O'Connor.text: Feargus Edward O'Connor was an Irish Chartist leader, MP and advocate of the Land Plan, which sought to provide smallholdings for the labouring classes. A highly charismatic figure, O'Connor was admired for his energy and oratory, but was criticised for alleged egotism. His newspaper Northern Star was widely read among workers, becoming the voice of the Chartist movement.
Feargus O'Connor.title: Feargus O'Connor

own.story: Feargus O'Connor, the leader of Chartism and owner of its newspaper, the Northern Star, was elected MP for Nottingham in 1847, defeating Thomas Benjamin Hobhouse.[^s1] His statue by J. B. Robinson was put up in the Arboretum in 1859.[^s2]

Florence Boot.text: Florence Anne Boot, Lady Trent was a Jersey businesswoman and philanthropist. She assisted her husband, Jesse Boot, in running Boots chemists after their marriage in 1886. Florence was responsible for diversifying the firm's retail offering to include perfume, cosmetics, stationery, books, and other general merchandise and also pioneered in-store cafés.
Florence Boot.title: Florence Boot

own.story: Florence Boot, born in St Helier, Jersey, in 1863, married Jesse Boot in 1886 and helped him run the firm. She brought books and stationery into the Goose Gate shop and started Boots Book-Lovers' Library and cafés in the stores. She founded the university's first hall for women, named Florence Boot Hall after her.

Frank Bowden.text: Sir Frank Bowden, 1st Baronet, was a British businessman and inventor. He was a founder of the Raleigh Bicycle Company.
Frank Bowden.title: Sir Frank Bowden, 1st Baronet

own.story: Frank Bowden took up cycling on his doctor's advice, bought a bicycle from a small workshop in Raleigh Street and in 1887–88 took control of the firm, then making three bicycles a week. He built it into the Raleigh company, and was made a baronet in 1915.

George Brough.text: George Brough was a motorcycle racer and a world record–holding motorcycle and automobile manufacturer and showman. He was known for his powerful and expensive Brough Superior motorcycles which were the first superbikes. George died in 1970 but his legacy lives on in the many Brough Superior motorcycles maintained by enthusiasts to this day.
George Brough.title: George Brough

own.story: George Brough was born in Basford on 21 April 1890 and set up his Brough Superior works on Haydn Road in 1919.[^s1] H. D. Teague of The Motor Cycle called the machines the "Rolls-Royce of Motorcycles".[^s2] T. E. Lawrence owned eight and died of injuries from a crash on the seventh.[^s2] War work ended production in 1940.[^s1][^s2] The pin is approximate.

George Green.text: George Green was a British mathematical physicist born in Sneinton, Nottinghamshire, now part of the city of Nottingham. Despite receiving little recognition during his lifetime, he is best remembered for his Essay on electricity and magnetism published in 1828.
George Green.title: George Green (mathematician)

own.story: George Green, the mathematician, was a miller: his family's windmill in Sneinton is restored and named after him.[^s1] He was a member of the subscription library at Bromley House.[^s1][^s2]

Godfrey Chetwynd, 8th Viscount Chetwynd.text: Godfrey John Boyle Chetwynd, 8th Viscount Chetwynd, CH was a British peer and industrialist, a member of the House of Lords from 1911 until his death. Chetwynd was the second son of Captain Henry Weyland Chetwynd and his wife Julia Bosville Davidson. On 12 April 1893, he married Baroness Hilda von Alvensleben-Rusteberg.
Godfrey Chetwynd, 8th Viscount Chetwynd.title: Godfrey Chetwynd, 8th Viscount Chetwynd

Harold Larwood.text: Harold Larwood was a cricketer for Nottinghamshire County Cricket Club and the England cricket team between 1924 and 1938. A right-arm fast bowler who combined extreme speeds with great accuracy, he was considered by many players and commentators to be the finest and the fastest fast bowler of his generation and one of the fastest bowlers of all time.
Harold Larwood.title: Harold Larwood

own.story: Harold Larwood, born at Nuncargate in 1904, played for Nottinghamshire from 1924 and bowled for England in the Bodyline series. He moved to Australia in 1950; Trent Bridge named the Larwood and Voce Stand after him and Bill Voce in 1985.

Harry Cursham.text: Henry Alfred Cursham was an English footballer and cricketer. He played football mostly for Notts County, with spells at Corinthian, Grantham Town and Thursday Wanderers. In cricket, he played two first class games for Nottinghamshire.
Harry Cursham.title: Harry Cursham

own.story: Harry Cursham was born in Wilford on 27 November 1859. In the FA Cup he scored 49 goals in 44 games for Notts County, the competition's individual scoring record, and for England 5 goals in 8 games; he also played two first-class cricket matches for Nottinghamshire. He died on 6 August 1941. The pin is approximate.

Henry Kirke White.text: Henry Kirke White was an English poet and hymn-writer. He died at the young age of 21.
Henry Kirke White.title: Henry Kirke White

own.story: The poet lived in Wilford in 1804–1805; the church holds two memorials to him.[^s1][^s2]

Henry Pelham-Clinton, 4th Duke of Newcas.text: Henry Pelham Fiennes Pelham-Clinton, 4th Duke of Newcastle-under-Lyne, was a British nobleman and politician who played a leading part in British politics in the late 1820s and early 1830s. He was styled Lord Clinton from birth until 1794 and Earl of Lincoln between 1794 and 1795.
Henry Pelham-Clinton, 4th Duke of Newcas.title: Henry Pelham-Clinton, 4th Duke of Newcastle

Herbert Kilpin.text: Herbert Kilpin was an English football player and manager, best known as the main founding father of AC Milan. After playing as an amateur in his native city of Nottingham, in the early 1890s he moved to Italy to work in the textile industry and he became one of the pioneers of football in the country, first as a player for Internazionale Torino and then as player, manager, and charter member of Milan.
Herbert Kilpin.title: Herbert Kilpin

own.story: Herbert Kilpin, a butcher's son, grew up here with nine older siblings, at what was then 129 Mansfield Road. He became the main founding father of AC Milan.

James Gandon.text: James Gandon was an English architect best known for his work in Ireland during the late 18th and early 19th centuries. His best known works include the Custom House, Beresford Place, Four Courts and King's Inns in Dublin and Emo Court in County Laois.
James Gandon.title: James Gandon

own.story: The architect James Gandon designed the rebuilt Shire Hall.[^s1][^s2]

James Iremonger.text: James Iremonger was an English cricketer and one of the players most unlucky never to play Test cricket. He did play a number of minor matches on the 1911–12 Ashes tour and was considered many times between 1901 and 1905 for a place against Australia.
James Iremonger.title: James Iremonger

own.story: James Iremonger was born in Norton, in the East Riding of Yorkshire, on 5 March 1876, and played for Wilford's football club in 1893.[^s1] He played for Nottingham Forest from 1895 to 1910, won two England caps in 1901–02, played cricket for Nottinghamshire from 1899 to 1914 and coached the county from 1921 to 1938.[^s1] His brother was Albert Iremonger, the Notts County goalkeeper.[^s1][^s2] He died in Nottingham on 25 March 1956.[^s1]

Jesse Boot.text: Jesse Boot, 1st Baron Trent transformed The Boots Company, founded by his father, John Boot, into a national retailer, which branded itself as "Chemists to the Nation".
Jesse Boot.title: Jesse Boot, 1st Baron Trent

own.story: Almshouses paid for by Jesse Boot, founder of Boots, in 1908 for veterans of the Crimean War and the Indian Mutiny: the Dorothy Boot Homes in Wilford.[^s1]

John Hutchinson.text: Colonel John Hutchinson was an English politician and army officer who played a significant role during the English Civil War. He was a Member of the House of Commons of England from 1646 to 1653 and briefly in 1660. Hutchinson was a prominent Puritan leader and served in the parliamentary army.
John Hutchinson.title: John Hutchinson (Roundhead)

own.story: John Hutchinson, born at Owthorpe in 1615, held Nottingham Castle for Parliament from 1643 and signed Charles I's death warrant.[^s1] He died a prisoner in 1664 and is buried at Owthorpe; his wife Lucy's Memoirs of his life made him famous.[^s1]

Lucy Hutchinson.text: Lucy Hutchinson was an English translator, poet, and biographer, and the first person to translate the complete text of Lucretius's De rerum natura into English verse, during the years of the Interregnum.
Lucy Hutchinson.title: Lucy Hutchinson

own.story: Lucy Hutchinson, born in the Tower of London in 1620, was the first to translate the whole of Lucretius into English verse, and her Order and Disorder is perhaps the first epic poem by a woman in English. Her life of her husband, John Hutchinson, written for her family, was printed in 1806. She died at Owthorpe in 1681.

Marriott Ogle Tarbotton.text: Marriott Ogle Tarbotton MICE, FGS, FRMS, was born in Leeds on 6 December 1834 and died in Nottingham on 6 March 1887. He was Borough Engineer for Nottingham from 1859.
Marriott Ogle Tarbotton.title: Marriott Ogle Tarbotton

own.story: Marriott Ogle Tarbotton was Nottingham's Borough Engineer from 1859. He designed Trent Bridge, planned the town's underground sewers, culverted the River Leen and built the viaduct over the railway on Carrington Street in 1866.

Mary Howitt.text: Mary Howitt was an English writer, editor, translator and a pioneer of the women's rights movement in the UK. She is most known as the author of the famous poem The Spider and the Fly. Howitt translated several works by Hans Christian Andersen and Frederika Bremer.
Mary Howitt.title: Mary Howitt

own.story: Mary Howitt married William Howitt in 1821, and by 1823 they were living in Nottingham, on Timber Hill, now South Parade, next to Smith's Bank, for over twelve years.[^house] She wrote The Spider and the Fly and translated Hans Christian Andersen's tales.

Mary Kendrick.text: Mary Patricia Kendrick MBE born Mary Patricia Boak was a British tidal engineer who was an expert on silt. She worked on many projects but she is known for leading a team working on the Thames Barrier. She broke a 200 year long list of Admirals who looked after keeping the River Mersey navigable when she appointed Acting Conservator of the River Mersey - a role that dates back to 1625.
Mary Kendrick.title: Mary Kendrick

own.story: Mary Kendrick, the tidal engineer who led the studies of river levels and silt for the Thames Barrier, grew up on Curzon Street, where her father was a haulage contractor. She later kept the Mersey navigable as its Acting Conservator.

Mary Potter.text: The Little Company of Mary, also known as the Blue Sisters, is a Catholic religious institute of women dedicated to caring for the suffering, the sick, and the dying. The order was founded in 1877 in Nottingham, England by Mary Potter.
Mary Potter.title: Little Company of Mary

own.story: In 1877 Mary Potter's Little Company of Mary began in an abandoned factory in Hyson Green. The sisters' main work was caring for the sick and dying. The pin is approximate.

Paul Smith.text: Sir Paul Brierley Smith is an English fashion designer, best known for his eponymous luxury brand. Founded by Smith in 1970, it has since expanded to 130 stores in more than 60 countries. The brand sells clothing and accessories through both physical shops and online.
Paul Smith.title: Paul Smith (fashion designer)

own.story: Paul Smith was born in Beeston on 5 July 1946. In 1970 he opened his first shop, Paul Smith Vêtements Pour Homme, at 6 Byard Lane, with a floor of only twelve feet by twelve feet. He was knighted in 2000.

Peter Mansfield.text: Sir Peter Mansfield was an English physicist who was awarded the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, shared with Paul Lauterbur, for discoveries concerning Magnetic Resonance Imaging. Mansfield was a professor at the University of Nottingham.
Peter Mansfield.title: Peter Mansfield

Peter Moro.text: Peter Meinhard Moro was a London-based architect whose practice developed many notable public buildings. He was the son of Slovenian physician and paediatrician Ernst Moro.
Peter Moro.title: Peter Moro

own.story: The architect Peter Moro designed the Playhouse.[^s1][^s2]

Richard Arkwright.text: Sir Richard Arkwright was an English inventor and a leading entrepreneur during the early Industrial Revolution. He is credited as the driving force behind the development of the spinning frame, known as the water frame after it was adapted to use water power; and he patented a rotary carding engine to convert raw cotton to 'cotton lap' prior to spinning. He was the first to develop factories housing both mechanised carding and spinning operations.
Richard Arkwright.title: Richard Arkwright

Samuel Morley.text: Samuel Morley, was an English woollen manufacturer and political radical. He is known as a philanthropist, Congregationalist dissenter, abolitionist, and statesman.
Samuel Morley.title: Samuel Morley (MP)

own.story: Samuel Morley, of the Nottingham hosiery firm I. & R. Morley, was elected MP for Nottingham in 1865 and endowed Morley College in London.[^s1] His memorial by Joseph Else stands at the Arboretum.[^s1]

Stewart Adams.text: Stewart Adams may refer to: Stewart Adams, Canadian ice hockey player Stewart Adams, English pharmacist
Stewart Adams.title: Stewart Adams

Thomas Adams.text: Thomas Adams was a British lace manufacturer and philanthropist based in Nottingham.
Thomas Adams.title: Thomas Adams (manufacturer and philanthropist)

own.story: The lace manufacturer Thomas Adams built this showroom and warehouse; it is named after him.[^s1][^s2]

Thomas Cecil Howitt.text: Thomas Cecil Howitt, OBE was a British provincial architect of the 20th Century. Howitt is chiefly remembered for designing prominent public buildings, such as the Council House and Processional Way in Nottingham, Baskerville House in Birmingham, Newport Civic Centre, and several Odeon cinemas. Howitt's chief architectural legacies are in his home city of Nottingham.
Thomas Cecil Howitt.title: Thomas Cecil Howitt

own.story: The architect Thomas Cecil Howitt designed the Council House.[^s1][^s2]

Thomas Chambers Hine.text: Thomas Chambers Hine was an architect based in Nottingham.
Thomas Chambers Hine.title: Thomas Chambers Hine

own.story: The Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine designed this lace showroom and warehouse.[^s1][^s2]

Tinsley Lindley.text: His Honour Tinsley Lindley, OBE was an English footballer. He was described as "an ideal centre forward". He scored three goals in his debut aged 16 for Nottingham Forest.
Tinsley Lindley.title: Tinsley Lindley

own.story: Tinsley Lindley, who played for Nottingham Forest and England and became a county court judge, lived here with his family at 14 Park Terrace.

Torvill and Dean.text: Torvill and Dean are British ice dancers and former British, European, Olympic, and World champions. At the Sarajevo 1984 Winter Olympics the pair won gold and became the highest-scoring figure skaters of all time for a single programme, receiving twelve perfect 6.0s and six 5.9s which included artistic impression scores of 6.0 from every judge, after skating to Maurice Ravel's Boléro.
Torvill and Dean.title: Torvill and Dean

own.story: The ice dancers Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean come from Nottingham.[^s1][^s2][^s3] The square outside the ice centre is named Bolero Square after their Olympic routine.[^s1][^s2][^s3] Jayne Torvill was born in Clifton on 7 October 1957 and worked as an insurance clerk at Norwich Union before skating full-time; at Sarajevo in 1984 she and Christopher Dean won the gold with their free dance to Ravel's Boléro, which earned twelve perfect 6.0 marks.[^s3]

Viv Anderson.text: Vivian Alexander Anderson is an English former professional footballer who played as a right-back. He is best known for his ten-year stint with Nottingham Forest, with whom he won the First Division title in 1978, as well as the European Cup in 1979 and 1980. In 1978, he became the first black footballer to play for England's senior men's national team, and from 1980 to 1988, was selected in the England squad for four major tournaments.
Viv Anderson.title: Viv Anderson

own.story: Viv Anderson was born in Clifton on 29 July 1956. In ten years at Nottingham Forest, from 1974 to 1984, he played 328 times and won the European Cup twice. In November 1978, against Czechoslovakia, he became the first black footballer to play for England's senior men's team.

W. G. Grace.text: William Gilbert Grace was an English cricketer who is widely held to have been one of the sport's all-time greatest players. Always known by his initials as "WG", his first-class career spanned a record-equalling 44 seasons from 1865 to 1908. Test cricket originated during his career, and he represented England in 22 matches from 1880 to 1899.
W. G. Grace.title: W. G. Grace

Wilfred Rhodes.text: Wilfred Rhodes was an English professional cricketer who played 58 Test matches for England between 1899 and 1930. In Tests, Rhodes took 127 wickets and scored 2,325 runs, becoming the first Englishman to complete the double of 1,000 runs and 100 wickets in Test matches. He holds the world records both for the most appearances made in first-class cricket and the most wickets taken.
Wilfred Rhodes.title: Wilfred Rhodes

William Howitt.text: William Howitt, was a prolific English writer on history and other subjects. Howitt Primary Community School in Heanor, Derbyshire, is named after him and his wife.
William Howitt.title: William Howitt

own.story: William Howitt, born in Heanor, made his home in Nottingham with Mary Howitt and was an alderman of the town, before they moved to Esher in 1837. In 1852 he sailed to Melbourne with two of his sons.

William Lee.text: William Lee was an English inventor and alleged clergyman who invented the stocking frame knitting machine. Framework knitting, as the use of Lee's machine in stocking production was called, was the first major stage in the mechanisation of the textile industry, a process that 200 years later precipitated the Industrial Revolution.
William Lee.title: William Lee (inventor)

William Thompson.text: William Abednego Thompson, also known as Bendigo Thompson and mononymously as Bendigo, was an English bare-knuckle boxer who won the heavyweight championship of England from James Burke on 12 February 1839. He was inducted into The Ring magazine Hall of Fame in 1955, the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1991 and the Bare Knuckle Boxing Hall of Fame in 2011. His nickname of "Bendigo" lives on in the name of a city and creek in Australia.
William Thompson.title: William Thompson (boxer)

own.story: William "Bendigo" Thompson, born in Nottingham on 11 October 1811, won the heavyweight championship of England in 1839. He died in 1880 and was buried in St Mary's burial ground, under a tomb with a crouching lion. The city of Bendigo in Australia is indirectly named after him.

John Leavers.text: John Levers was an English mechanic and engineer, best known for improving John Heathcoat’s pioneering lace machine; the Leavers machine laid the foundation of the machine lace trade.
John Leavers.title: John Levers

Watson Fothergill.text: Watson Fothergill was a British architect who designed over 100 unique buildings in Nottingham in the East Midlands of England. His influences were mainly from the Gothic Revival and Old English vernacular architecture styles. His work dates from 1864 to around 1912.
Watson Fothergill.title: Watson Fothergill

John Wesley.text: John Wesley was an English cleric, theologian, and evangelist who was a principal leader of a revival movement within the Church of England known as Methodism. The societies he founded became the dominant form of the ongoing independent Methodist movement. Educated at Charterhouse and Christ Church, Oxford, Wesley was elected a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1726 and ordained as an Anglican priest two years later.
John Wesley.title: John Wesley

John Player.text: John Player & Sons, most often known simply as Player's, was a tobacco and cigarette manufacturer based in Nottingham, England. In 1901 the company merged with twelve other companies to become a branch of the Imperial Tobacco Company of Great Britain and Ireland. The company pioneered the advertising with trading cards.
John Player.title: John Player & Sons

Charles I.text: Charles I was King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 27 March 1625 until his execution in 1649. Charles was born into the House of Stuart as the second son of King James VI of Scotland. After his father inherited the English throne in 1603, he moved to England, where he spent much of the rest of his life.
Charles I.title: Charles I of England

Samuel Bourne.text: Samuel Bourne was a British photographer known for his prolific seven years' work in India, from 1863 to 1870. Together with Charles Shepherd, he set up Bourne & Shepherd first in Shimla in 1863 and later in Kolkata; the company closed in June 2016.
Samuel Bourne.title: Samuel Bourne

William Ewart Gladstone.text: William Ewart Gladstone was a British statesman who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom for four non-consecutive terms between 1868 and 1894, the most of any British prime minister. He began in politics as a Conservative Member of Parliament for Newark and ended as the face of the Liberal Party.
William Ewart Gladstone.title: William Ewart Gladstone

Arthur Mee.text: Arthur Henry Mee was an English writer, journalist and educator. He is best known for The Harmsworth Self-Educator, The Children's Encyclopædia, The Children's Newspaper, and The King's England.
Arthur Mee.title: Arthur Mee

Laura Knight.text: Dame Laura Knight was an English artist who worked in oils, watercolours, etching, engraving and drypoint. Knight was a painter in the figurative, realist tradition, who embraced English Impressionism. In her long career, Knight was among the most successful and popular painters in Britain.
Laura Knight.title: Laura Knight

Marshal Tallard.text: Camille d'Hostun de la Baume, duc de Tallard was a French nobleman, diplomat and military commander, who became a Marshal of France.
Marshal Tallard.title: Camille d'Hostun, duc de Tallard

Charles Blacker Vignoles.text: Charles Blacker Vignoles was an Irish railway engineer, and eponym of the Vignoles rail.
Charles Blacker Vignoles.title: Charles Blacker Vignoles

Frank Matcham.text: Francis Matcham was an English architect who specialised in the design of theatres and music halls. He worked extensively in London, predominantly under Moss Empires for whom he designed the Hippodrome in 1900, Hackney Empire, Shepherd's Bush Empire, Coliseum, and Palladium. His last major commission before retirement was the Victoria Palace Theatre in 1911 for the variety magnate Alfred Butt.
Frank Matcham.title: Frank Matcham

Thomas Rickman.text: Thomas Rickman was an English architect and architectural antiquary who was a major figure in the Gothic Revival. He is particularly remembered for his Attempt to Discriminate the Styles of English Architecture, which established the basic chronological classification and terminology that are still in widespread use for the different styles of English medieval ecclesiastical architecture.
Thomas Rickman.title: Thomas Rickman

George Frederick Bodley.text: George Frederick Bodley was an English Gothic Revival architect. He was a pupil of Sir George Gilbert Scott and worked with C. E.
George Frederick Bodley.title: George Frederick Bodley

Vincent Harris.text: Emanuel Vincent Harris, often known as E. Vincent Harris, was an English architect who designed several important public buildings in traditional styles.
Vincent Harris.title: E. Vincent Harris

Arthur Brewill.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Arthur William Lancelot Brewill was an architect based in Nottingham.
Arthur Brewill.title: Arthur Brewill

Alexander Wilson.text: Alexander Wilson LRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham. Some of his most significant work include the 900 houses built on the Beeston Rylands estate in the late 1930s.
Alexander Wilson.title: Alexander Wilson (British architect)

George Gilbert Scott.text: Sir George Gilbert Scott, largely known as Sir Gilbert Scott, was a prolific English Gothic Revival architect, chiefly associated with the design, building and renovation of churches and cathedrals, although he started his career as a leading designer of workhouses. Over 800 buildings were designed or altered by him.
George Gilbert Scott.title: George Gilbert Scott

William James Morley.text: William James Morley FRIBA was an English architect who practised from offices in Bolton, Greater Manchester and Bradford, West Yorkshire.
William James Morley.title: William James Morley

John Wills.text: John Wills was an architect based in Derby.
John Wills.title: John Wills (architect)

Owen Williams.text: Sir Evan Owen Williams was a British engineer and architect, known for being the principal engineer for the original Wembley Stadium, and later Gravelly Hill Interchange as well as a number of key modernist buildings, including the Express Building in Manchester and the D10 and D6 Buildings at the Boots Factory Site in Nottingham.
Owen Williams.title: Owen Williams (engineer)

William Herbert Higginbottom.text: William Herbert Higginbottom JP was an architect based in Nottingham.
William Herbert Higginbottom.title: William Herbert Higginbottom

Richard Charles Sutton.text: Richard Charles Sutton was an architect based in Nottingham. He was born 1834 and died on 18 October 1915. He was a member of Nottingham City Council from 1887 to 1901.
Richard Charles Sutton.title: Richard Charles Sutton

Charles Trubshaw.text: Charles Trubshaw FRIBA was an architect specifically associated with railway buildings on the London and North Western Railway and Midland Railway lines.
Charles Trubshaw.title: Charles Trubshaw

Albert Edward Lambert.text: Albert Edward Lambert, FRIBA was a British architect based in Nottingham, England.
Albert Edward Lambert.title: Albert Edward Lambert

Robert Evans JP.text: Robert Evans FRIBA, JP was an English architect based in Nottingham.
Robert Evans JP.title: Robert Evans (architect, 1832–1911)

Peter Frederick Robinson.text: Peter Frederick Robinson was an English architect.
Peter Frederick Robinson.title: Peter Frederick Robinson

Stockdale Harrison.text: Stockdale Harrison FRIBA was an architect based in Leicester best known for Usher Hall, Edinburgh.
Stockdale Harrison.title: Stockdale Harrison

Thomas Simpson.text: Thomas Simpson was an English architect based in Nottingham.
Thomas Simpson.title: Thomas Simpson (architect, born 1816)

William Arthur Heazell.text: William Arthur Heazell FRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham.
William Arthur Heazell.title: William Arthur Heazell

Caruso St John.text: Caruso St John is a British architectural practice founded in 1990 by Adam Caruso and Peter St John. The firm first came to wider attention with The New Art Gallery Walsall, completed after an international competition win in 1995, and has since worked across a broad range of public and private projects. Caruso St John won the RIBA Stirling Prize in 2016 for Newport Street Gallery, having previously been shortlisted in 2000 and 2006.
Caruso St John.title: Caruso St John

Basil Baily.text: Captain Basil Edgar Baily FRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham. Much of his earlier work had to do with nearby churches.
Basil Baily.title: Basil Baily

Stuart Colman.text: Stuart Colman was an architect based in Bristol and London, England.
Stuart Colman.title: Stuart Colman (architect)

Edward James Willson.text: Edward James Willson was an English architect, antiquary, architectural writer, and mayor of Lincoln in 1851–2.
Edward James Willson.title: Edward James Willson

Gilbert Smith Doughty.text: Captain Gilbert Smith Doughty CE was an architect based in Nottingham and Matlock.
Gilbert Smith Doughty.title: Gilbert Smith Doughty

John Howitt.text: John Howitt FRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham.
John Howitt.title: John Howitt

John Collyer.text: John Collyer was an architect based in Nottingham.
John Collyer.title: John Collyer

RHWL.text: RHWL Architects was a British architecture practice based in London, Berlin and Qatar. It was created by Andrew Renton, Peter Howard and Humphrey Wood following the establishment of Andrew Renton & Associates in 1961. Gerald Levin became a Name Partner in 1973, and from that date the Firm was often known as 'RHWL'.
RHWL.title: RHWL

Thomas Verity.text: Thomas Verity was an English theatre architect during the theatre-building boom of 1885–1915. Verity began his career articled in the architecture department of the War Office, assisting in the erection of the South Kensington Museum. He further assisted in the building of the Royal Albert Hall between 1867 and 1870.
Thomas Verity.title: Thomas Verity

Henry Isaac Stevens.text: Henry Isaac Stevens FRIBA was an architect based in Derby. He was born in London, in 1806, and died in 1873. In the late 1850s he changed his name to Isaac Henry Stevens.
Henry Isaac Stevens.title: Henry Isaac Stevens

Samuel Sutton Rawlinson.text: Samuel Sutton Rawlinson was an architect and engineer known for his work in Nottingham.
Samuel Sutton Rawlinson.title: Samuel Sutton Rawlinson

Robert Smythson.text: Robert Smythson was an English architect. Smythson designed a number of notable houses during the Elizabethan era. Little is known about his birth and upbringing—his first mention in historical records comes in 1556, when he was stonemason for the house at Longleat, built by Sir John Thynne.
Robert Smythson.title: Robert Smythson

John Johnson.text: John Johnson was an English architect who specialised in religious buildings and churches in the Gothic style. He was regularly employed by the civil engineer Sir John Kelk to design the homes and public buildings Kelk funded.
John Johnson.title: John Johnson (architect, born 1807)

F. W. Dixon & Son.text: Frederick Whittaker Dixon was an architect practising in Oldham, Lancashire.
F. W. Dixon & Son.title: Frederick Whittaker Dixon

William Douglas Caroe.text: William Douglas Caröe was a British architect, particularly of churches.
William Douglas Caroe.title: W. D. Caröe

William Bradford.text: William Bradford was a prolific English architect of breweries.
William Bradford.title: William Bradford (architect)

Herbert Walker.text: Lieut-Colonel Herbert Walker FRIBA, M Inst CE, FSI, was an architect, surveyor and civil engineer based in Nottingham from 1870 to 1923.
Herbert Walker.title: Herbert Walker (architect)

Ernest Richard Eckett Sutton.text: Ernest Richard Eckett Sutton FRIBA was an English architect based in Nottingham.
Ernest Richard Eckett Sutton.title: Ernest Richard Eckett Sutton

Gerard Goalen.text: Gerard Thomas Goalen was a British architect who specialised in church architecture and was influenced by continental models and the Liturgical Movement. He was one of the most important architects of the Catholic Modernist movement in the United Kingdom during the 20th century.
Gerard Goalen.title: Gerard Goalen

John Loughborough Pearson.text: John Loughborough Pearson was a British Gothic Revival architect renowned for his work on churches and cathedrals. Pearson revived and practised largely the art of vaulting, and acquired in it a proficiency unrivalled in his generation. He worked on at least 210 ecclesiastical buildings in England alone in a career spanning 54 years.
John Loughborough Pearson.title: John Loughborough Pearson

Thomas Oliver.text: Thomas Oliver was an English classical architect and surveyor active in Newcastle upon Tyne. He was one of the numerous local architects who worked with Richard Grainger on the development of Newcastle, but his work tends to be overshadowed by that of John Dobson, who has been given a great deal of the credit for the central part of the city referred to as Grainger Town.
Thomas Oliver.title: Thomas Oliver (architect)

John Carr.text: John Carr was an English architect. He is best known for Buxton Crescent in Derbyshire and Harewood House in West Yorkshire. Much of his work was in the Palladian style.
John Carr.title: John Carr (architect)

William Booth.text: William Booth was an English Methodist preacher who, along with his wife, Catherine, founded the Salvation Army and became its first General. This Christian movement, founded in 1865, has a quasi-military structure and government and has spread from London to many parts of the world. It is one of the largest distributors of humanitarian aid.
William Booth.title: William Booth

own.story: William Booth, who founded the Salvation Army, was born in this house in Notintone Place, Sneinton. It is now the William Booth Birthplace Museum, telling the story of Booth, his wife Catherine and their family.

Ged Walker.text: PC Gerald Michael "Ged" Walker was an English police dog handler with Nottinghamshire Police who was killed in the line of duty in Bulwell, Nottingham, in 2003. On 7 January 2003, PC Walker was dragged 100 yards and fatally injured by a stolen taxi as he reached into the vehicle in an attempt to remove the keys from the ignition. He died in hospital two days later from serious head injuries.
Ged Walker.title: Death of Ged Walker

George Africanus.text: George John Scipio Africanus was a West African former slave who became a successful entrepreneur in Nottingham, England.
George Africanus.title: George Africanus

Frank Robinson.text: Frank Robinson was an eccentric street entertainer in Nottingham, England. He was by far Nottingham's best known busker and was regularly seen around Nottingham City Centre for over fifteen years. His favourite busking place was outside of the C&A store in the Lister Gate area of the city.
Frank Robinson.title: Frank Robinson (Xylophone Man)

Thomas Humber.text: Thomas Humber was an English engineer and cycle manufacturer who developed and patented a safety bicycle with a diamond-shaped frame and wheels of similar size. It became a pattern for subsequent machines. Humber made many other improvements to bicycles.
Thomas Humber.title: Thomas Humber

Edward Joseph Lowe.text: Edward Joseph Lowe FRS FGS FRAS FLS was a British botanist, meteorologist and astronomer, who published papers on a wide variety of subjects, including luminous meteors, sunspots, the zodiacal light, meteorological observations during the 1860 solar eclipse, conchology, ferns, grasses and other plants.
Edward Joseph Lowe.title: Edward Joseph Lowe

John Clifford.text: John Clifford was a British Baptist Nonconformist minister and politician, who became famous as the advocate of passive resistance to the Education Act 1902.
John Clifford.title: John Clifford (minister)

William Frederick Wallett.text: William Frederick "W.F." Wallett was a popular circus clown in Victorian England, who also enjoyed modest celebrity in the United States. After he performed before Queen Victoria in 1844 at Windsor Castle, Wallett began promoting himself as "the Queen's Jester", and described himself this way in the title of his 1870 autobiography. For many years, he performed in the circus owned by his good friend Pablo Fanque Wallett also helped manage Fanque's circus.
William Frederick Wallett.title: W. F. Wallett

Richard Beckinsale.text: Richard Arthur Beckinsale was an English actor. He played Lennie Godber in the BBC sitcoms Porridge and Going Straight, and Alan Moore in the ITV sitcom Rising Damp. He was the father of actresses Samantha and Kate Beckinsale.
Richard Beckinsale.title: Richard Beckinsale

Gilbert Wakefield.text: Gilbert Wakefield was an English scholar and controversialist. He moved from being a cleric and academic, into tutoring at dissenting academies, and finally became a professional writer and publicist. In a celebrated state trial, he was imprisoned for a pamphlet critical of government policy of the French Revolutionary Wars; and died shortly after his release.
Gilbert Wakefield.title: Gilbert Wakefield

Albert Ball.text: Albert Ball, was a British fighter pilot during the First World War. At the time of his death he was the United Kingdom's leading flying ace, with 44 victories, and remained its fourth-highest scorer behind Edward Mannock, James McCudden and George McElroy. Born and raised in Nottingham, Ball joined the Sherwood Foresters at the outbreak of the First World War and was commissioned as a second lieutenant in October 1914.
Albert Ball.title: Albert Ball

T Cecil Howitt.text: Thomas Cecil Howitt, OBE was a British provincial architect of the 20th Century. Howitt is chiefly remembered for designing prominent public buildings, such as the Council House and Processional Way in Nottingham, Baskerville House in Birmingham, Newport Civic Centre, and several Odeon cinemas. Howitt's chief architectural legacies are in his home city of Nottingham.
T Cecil Howitt.title: Thomas Cecil Howitt

Alan Sillitoe.text: Alan Sillitoe FRSL was an English writer and one of the so-called "angry young men" of the 1950s. He disliked the label, as did most of the other writers to whom it was applied. He is best known for his debut novel Saturday Night and Sunday Morning and his early short story "The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner", both of which were adapted into films.
Alan Sillitoe.title: Alan Sillitoe

own.story: A plaque on this house, 38 Manton Crescent in Lenton Abbey, says that the writer Alan Sillitoe was born here on 4 March 1928.

Helen Watts.text: Helen Kirkpatrick Watts was a militant British suffragette from Nottingham.
Helen Watts.title: Helen Kirkpatrick Watts

own.story: Helen Watts, the daughter of the vicar of Lenton, joined Nottingham's suffragettes after hearing Christabel Pankhurst speak in 1907. In 1909 she served a month in Holloway, was arrested here at the Albert Hall in July and let go without charge, and went on hunger strike in Leicester gaol.

Nellie Crocker.text: Ellen Crocker was an English suffragette.
Nellie Crocker.title: Ellen Crocker

own.story: Nellie Crocker was the suffragettes' organiser in Nottingham from 1909 to 1912, with an office on Carlton Street. After her eighth arrest, for attacking a post office in London, she spent three months of 1912 in Holloway.

Richard Parkes Bonington.text: Richard Parkes Bonington was an English Romantic landscape painter, who in his last years also painted many historical figure paintings. His family moved to France when he was 14 and he can also be considered as a French artist, and an intermediary bringing aspects of English style to France.
Richard Parkes Bonington.title: Richard Parkes Bonington

own.story: A plaque on this house, 79 High Street in Arnold, says that the artist Richard Parkes Bonington was born here on 26 October 1802.

Philip James Bailey.text: Philip James Bailey was an English poet, best known as the author of Festus.
Philip James Bailey.title: Philip James Bailey

J. M. Barrie.text: Sir James Matthew Barrie, 1st Baronet was a Scottish novelist and playwright. He was born and educated in Scotland and then moved to London, where he wrote several successful novels and plays.
J. M. Barrie.title: J. M. Barrie

Lord Byron.text: George Noel Gordon Byron, 6th Baron Byron, known as Lord Byron was a British poet. He was one of the major figures of the Romantic movement, and is regarded as being among the greatest British poets. Among his best known works are the lengthy narratives Don Juan and Childe Harold's Pilgrimage; many of his shorter lyrics in Hebrew Melodies also became popular.
Lord Byron.title: Lord Byron

Henry Dawson.text: Henry Dawson was a British landscape painter. Born in Kingston upon Hull, Dawson went with his parents to Nottingham when he was still an infant and always regarded the latter as his native town. His parents were poor, and he began life in a Nottingham lace factory.
Henry Dawson.title: Henry Dawson (artist)

John Borlase Warren.text: Admiral of the White Sir John Borlase Warren, 1st Baronet was a Royal Navy officer, diplomat and politician who sat in the British House of Commons between 1774 and 1807.
John Borlase Warren.title: John Borlase Warren

Graham Greene.text: Henry Graham Greene was an English writer and journalist regarded by many as one of the leading novelists of the 20th century. Combining literary acclaim with widespread popularity, Greene acquired a reputation early in his lifetime as a major writer, both of serious Catholic novels, and of thrillers. He was shortlisted for the Nobel Prize in Literature several times.
Graham Greene.title: Graham Greene

William Beedham Starr.text: William Beedham Starr JP was an architect based in Nottingham, England.
William Beedham Starr.title: William Beedham Starr

Joseph Warburton.text: Joseph Warburton LRIBA MRAIC was a 20th century architect based in Beeston, Nottinghamshire and Regina, Saskatchewan.
Joseph Warburton.title: Joseph Warburton

John Bowley.text: John Bowley LRIBA was an architect and engineer based in England who worked mainly in Beeston, Nottinghamshire and Hastings.
John Bowley.title: John Bowley

George Francis Grimwood.text: George Francis Grimwood LRIBA was a 20th-century engineer and architect based in Nottingham.
George Francis Grimwood.title: George Francis Grimwood

William Vallance Betts.text: William Vallance Betts LRIBA was an English architect based in Nottingham.
William Vallance Betts.title: William Vallance Betts

John Rigby Poyser.text: John Rigby Poyser LRIBA was an English architect based in Nottingham.
John Rigby Poyser.title: John Rigby Poyser

Ernest Reginald Ridgway.text: Ernest Reginald Ridgway was an English architect based in Long Eaton.
Ernest Reginald Ridgway.title: Ernest Reginald Ridgway

James Huckerby.text: James Huckerby was a 19th-century builder and architect based in Beeston, Nottingham.
James Huckerby.title: James Huckerby

Hedley John Price.text: Hedley John Price ARIBA was an English architect based in Nottingham.
Hedley John Price.title: Hedley John Price

Charles Nelson Holloway.text: Charles Nelson Holloway was an architect based in Nottingham.
Charles Nelson Holloway.title: Charles Nelson Holloway

Frederick Ball.text: Frederick Ball LRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham. He was Sheriff of Nottingham from 1906 to 1907, and Mayor of Nottingham from 1913 to 1914.

Ernest Hooley.text: Ernest Hooley LRIBA was an architect based in Long Eaton.
Ernest Hooley.title: Ernest Hooley

Jeffry Wyatville.text: Sir Jeffry Wyatville was an English architect and garden designer. Born Jeffry Wyatt into an established dynasty of architects, in 1824 he was allowed by King George IV to change his surname to Wyatville. He is mainly remembered for making alterations and extensions to Chatsworth House and Windsor Castle.
Jeffry Wyatville.title: Jeffry Wyatville

Lawrence Bright.text: Lawrence Bright was an architect based in Nottingham.
Lawrence Bright.title: Lawrence Bright

Samuel Dutton Walker.text: Samuel Dutton Walker F.S.A. was an architect based in Nottingham.
Samuel Dutton Walker.title: Samuel Dutton Walker

Arthur George Marshall.text: Arthur George Marshall ARIBA was an architect based in Nottingham from 1881.
Arthur George Marshall.title: Arthur George Marshall

Sir Robert Taylor.text: Sir Robert Taylor was an English architect and sculptor who worked in London and the south of England.
Sir Robert Taylor.title: Robert Taylor (architect)

Alfred Waterhouse.text: Alfred Waterhouse was an English architect, particularly associated with Gothic Revival architecture, although he designed using other architectural styles as well. He is perhaps best known for his designs for Manchester Town Hall and the Natural History Museum in London. He designed other town halls, the Manchester Assize buildings—bombed in World War II—and the adjacent Strangeways Prison.
Alfred Waterhouse.title: Alfred Waterhouse

Arthur Richard Calvert.text: Arthur Richard Calvert was an architect based in Nottingham.
Arthur Richard Calvert.title: Arthur Richard Calvert

William Stretton.text: William Stretton was a builder and architect based in Nottingham.
William Stretton.title: William Stretton

Alfred John Thraves.text: Alfred John Thraves FRIBA was an architect based in Nottingham who specialised in cinema design.
Alfred John Thraves.title: Alfred John Thraves

William Dymock Pratt.text: William Dymock Pratt was an architect based in Nottingham, England
William Dymock Pratt.title: William Dymock Pratt

Henry Moses Wood.text: Henry Moses Wood was an architect based in Nottingham.
Henry Moses Wood.title: Henry Moses Wood

own.story: Ann Morley, a businesswoman, built this house in 1750, a rare Georgian town house built by a woman. The Nottingham School of Design opened here in 1843, and in 1854 the lace merchant George Gill made it the People's Hall, an institute for working men.
Cassandra Willoughby (1670–1735) oversaw the restoration of Wollaton Hall and its gardens.
From 1913, at the Girls' Friendly Society hostel at 4–6 Regent Street, Constance Penswick Smith (1878–1938) worked to revive Mothering Sunday, with the hostel's superintendent, Ellen Porter.
Edith Ransom (1872–1949) was the first woman president of Bromley House Library.
Ellen Harrington was the first woman librarian of Bromley House, from 1943 to 1983. Her portrait hangs here, in a room named after her.

Helena Dowson ran Nottingham's suffrage society from 1895 and its shop on Long Row. In 1920 she became the first woman magistrate and a Liberal councillor for the Meadows; a plaque here at the Justice Centre remembers her.
Jessie Batten, a London graduate of 1892, owned Western House school here from 1895. She married in 1910 but kept her own name at work, and retired in 1918.
Kate Watson Wallis (1852–1918), a suffragist, lived in the Residence at the Castle with her husband, the Castle Art Gallery's first curator.

Louisa Clarke opened a day and boarding school for girls in 1874, at 9 Park Terrace; called Western House, it moved here, to 30 The Ropewalk, in 1890. Rose Feilmann, who wrote "There are fairies at the bottom of my garden", was one of her pupils.
Louisa May Long (1892–1981), who nursed with the 94 Nottingham VAD at Radcliffe on Trent in the First World War, was Matron of Florence Boot Hall from 1928 to 1946.

Margaret Glen-Bott (1891–1969) came to Nottingham in 1916. The first woman gynaecologist to be Honorary Surgeon at the Women's Hospital and the Children's Hospital, and later a magistrate, she lived at 15 Regent Street.
Ruth Bryan (1805–1860) came to Nottingham as a child with her father, a minister. She lived at 18 High Pavement and kept a detailed diary from 1822.

Sarah Gray, Nottingham's first woman GP, lived and practised at 21 Regent Street. At the Women's Hospital from 1899 she was refused charge of in-patients; in 1921 she became the first president of the Nottingham Medico-Chirurgical Society.

Vera Anderson, a Boots nurse, was on duty when bombs wrecked the Boots Printing Works here on 8 May 1941. She gave first aid to a dying night watchman through burning debris, then treated casualties at the control centre, and was awarded the George Medal.
